name: DNS Resolution System
description: Design a DNS resolution system. Covers recursive resolution, hierarchical caching, TTL-based invalidation, the root/TLD/authoritative server hierarchy, and DNS-based load balancing.

learnSteps.title: Recursive Resolution Process
learnSteps.description: When a client queries 'www.example.com', the recursive resolver checks its local cache first. On a miss, it queries the Root Name Server, which responds with the .com TLD server address. The resolver then queries the TLD server, which responds with example.com's authoritative server address. Finally, the authoritative server returns the actual IP address. Each response includes a TTL dictating how long to cache it.

learnSteps.title: Hierarchical Caching Strategy
learnSteps.description: DNS relies on aggressive caching at every level. The resolver caches responses with their TTL (typically 300s for A records, 86400s for NS records). Root and TLD responses are cached for days since they rarely change, while authoritative records use shorter TTLs for flexibility. A 90% cache hit rate means only 10% of queries trigger the full resolution chain, reducing latency from ~70ms to ~1ms for cached entries.

learnSteps.title: The Root Server Infrastructure
learnSteps.description: There are 13 logical root server clusters (A through M), operated by 12 independent organizations. Each cluster uses Anycast routing, so hundreds of physical servers worldwide respond to the same IP addresses. A client's query goes to the geographically nearest root server. This design provides both fault tolerance and low latency. Root servers only store pointers to TLD servers, not actual domain records.

learnSteps.title: DNS-Based Load Balancing and Failover
learnSteps.description: Authoritative servers can return multiple A records for round-robin load balancing, or use weighted records to distribute traffic unevenly. TTLs are set low (30-60s) for services requiring fast failover. Health-checked DNS (Route 53, Cloudflare) removes unhealthy endpoints from responses automatically. GeoDNS returns different IPs based on the resolver's location, routing users to the nearest data center.

chaosScenarios.name: Authoritative Zone Outage
chaosScenarios.description: The authoritative name servers for a major hosted zone stop responding — the Dyn 2016 / Facebook 2021 incident pattern
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Cached records keep resolving until their TTL expires, then queries for the zone return SERVFAIL. Client retry storms multiply resolver query volume 3-5x because failed resolutions are retried far more aggressively than successful ones.
mitigationSteps: Enable serve-stale (RFC 8767) so expired records keep answering for the duration of the outage
Apply per-source rate limits to cap retry amplification
Verify anycast/BGP announcements for the authoritative fleet before assuming application-level failure

chaosScenarios.name: Resolver Cache Flush
chaosScenarios.description: The shared DNS cache crashes and restarts cold, dropping the 90% hit rate to zero
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Every query walks the full root → TLD → authoritative chain. Median latency jumps from ~1ms to ~70ms, upstream query volume rises 10x, and resolver CPU climbs from recursion bookkeeping.
mitigationSteps: Warm the cache from a top-domains list before readmitting full traffic
Enable query coalescing so concurrent misses for the same name trigger a single upstream lookup
Temporarily raise the minimum cache TTL to accelerate refill

chaosScenarios.name: Random-Subdomain (Water Torture) DDoS
chaosScenarios.description: A botnet floods the resolver with queries for unique random labels (x7f2a.example.com), making every query an uncacheable miss aimed at the victim zone's authoritative servers
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Cache hit rate collapses by design, recursion queue depth grows on the resolver, and the victim zone's authoritative servers saturate. Legitimate queries for that zone begin timing out.
mitigationSteps: Enable aggressive NSEC caching (RFC 8198) to answer random labels from cached denial-of-existence proofs
Apply per-client query limits and response rate limiting (RRL)
Drop queries matching the random-label signature at the resolver edge

bottleneckProgression.description: UDP packet processing and recursion state tracking saturate resolver CPU
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale resolver instances horizontally behind anycast addresses

bottleneckProgression.description: Every query consults the shared cache first; Redis network throughput becomes the ceiling
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add an in-process L1 cache on each resolver; shard the shared cache by domain hash

bottleneckProgression.description: The 10% cache-miss stream plus attack noise saturates the 4-instance authoritative fleet
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add authoritative instances behind anycast and raise NS record TTLs to push load into downstream caches

expectedIssues.title: TTL-Expiry Stampede on Popular Domains
expectedIssues.description: When a heavily queried record expires, thousands of concurrent misses trigger duplicate recursion for the same name
expectedIssues.mitigation: Prefetch popular records shortly before TTL expiry and coalesce concurrent identical queries

expectedIssues.title: Stale Records After Origin IP Change
expectedIssues.description: A zone migrates to new IPs but resolvers worldwide serve the old A record until the full TTL elapses, sending users to a dead endpoint
expectedIssues.mitigation: Lower the record TTL to 60s at least one full TTL window before any planned migration

expectedIssues.title: Cache Poisoning via Spoofed UDP Responses
expectedIssues.description: An attacker races the authoritative answer with a forged UDP response to plant a malicious record in the shared cache
expectedIssues.mitigation: Source-port randomization, 0x20 query-name encoding, and DNSSEC validation on the resolver

expectedIssues.title: Resolver Tier as Single Point of Failure
expectedIssues.description: All client traffic funnels through one logical resolver tier; losing it takes every domain offline for clients regardless of authoritative health
expectedIssues.mitigation: Run resolvers at multiple anycast sites and publish two resolver IPs so client stub resolvers can fail over

components.label: Recursive Resolver Fleet

components.label: Authoritative Servers

steps: Run dig +trace against each listed NS to confirm whether the outage is zone-wide or per-server
Enable serve-stale on the resolver so expired records keep answering
Check anycast/BGP route health for the authoritative fleet
Contact the zone owner and extend stale-answer TTLs if the outage persists
Post a status update once blast radius is confirmed
Verify dns-cache cluster health, memory pressure, and recent restarts
Enable per-client recursion rate limits to protect upstream servers
Warm the cache from the top-domains list
Scale the resolver fleet to absorb the temporary recursion CPU load
Confirm the signature in query logs: high-entropy unique labels with NXDOMAIN answers
Enable response rate limiting and aggressive NSEC caching
Push per-client query caps to the resolver edge
Coordinate with the victim zone's operators on upstream filtering

decisions.title: TTL-Driven Hierarchical Caching
decisions.context: 100k QPS where most names are queried repeatedly; a full recursive walk costs ~70ms across three upstream round trips
decisions.decision: Honor zone-owner TTLs and cache every response at the resolver, using volatile-ttl eviction so expiry order follows record lifetimes
consequences: 90% of queries answered in ~1ms with zero upstream traffic
Record freshness is controlled by the zone owner's TTL, not the resolver operator

decisions.title: UDP-First Transport with TCP Fallback
decisions.context: Resolution sits on the critical path of nearly every network request, so per-query overhead must be minimal
decisions.decision: Serve queries over single-round-trip UDP, falling back to TCP only on truncated responses
consequences: Lowest possible latency for the common case
Spoofing exposure requires source-port randomization and DNSSEC validation as compensating controls

decisions.title: Shared Cache Tier Separate from Resolver Instances
decisions.context: Resolver instances are stateless and scale horizontally; a per-instance cache would fragment hit rates as the fleet grows
decisions.decision: Back all resolver instances with one shared Redis cache tier
consequences: Cache hit rate is independent of which resolver instance receives a query
The cache becomes a shared dependency that needs its own HA and capacity story

tradeoffs.choice: Cache aggressively for the full record TTL
tradeoffs.benefit: 10x reduction in upstream queries and ~1ms cached answers
tradeoffs.cost: IP changes propagate slowly; fast failover requires TTLs lowered in advance

tradeoffs.choice: Serve stale records when authoritative servers are unreachable
tradeoffs.benefit: Survives authoritative outages without a SERVFAIL storm
tradeoffs.cost: Can hand out addresses that no longer exist during an origin incident

alternatives.name: DNS-over-HTTPS Resolver
alternatives.description: Terminate DoH/TLS at the resolver edge instead of plain UDP
alternatives.prosVsCons: Privacy and spoofing resistance, but TLS handshakes and HTTP framing raise per-query compute and latency
alternatives.whyNotChosen: DoH layers onto this design without changing the cache hierarchy; the classic UDP path is the foundation to model first

alternatives.name: Client-Side Iterative Resolution
alternatives.description: Clients walk root, TLD, and authoritative servers themselves with no recursive resolver
alternatives.prosVsCons: Removes the resolver as a dependency, but destroys cache sharing and multiplies upstream load by the client count
alternatives.whyNotChosen: The shared recursive cache is the single largest latency and load win in DNS
